uncited: - Input: A scalar volume dataset $V$ defined on a regular 3D grid, and a sample position $\mathbf{p} = (x, y, z)$ within the volume bounds.
The implementation assumes standard grid indexing where $V(i, j, k)$ accesses the value at grid coordinates $(i, j, k)$.

**Interpolate Support Samples**: Since the sample point $\mathbf{p}$ is generally not aligned with grid nodes, the six scalar values required for the central difference stencil must be interpolated from the volume data.
Let $V_{\text{interp}}(x, y, z)$ denote the interpolated value at arbitrary coordinates.
- Interpolation Filter: The quality of the interpolation filter significantly impacts gradient accuracy.
- **Boundary Conditions**: When sample points are near volume boundaries, the stencil requires values outside the grid.
Poor interpolation can lead to noisy normals and incorrect shading.
Computes gradients at all grid nodes beforehand and stores them.
Uses more memory but reduces per-sample compute cost. [Gradient Selection — Central/Forward/Backward](12132-gradient-selection-central-forward-backward.md)
Applies optimized gradient filters directly to the volume data.
Often provides the best visual results but has higher complexity. [Gradient Selection — Central/Forward/Backward](12132-gradient-selection-central-forward-backward.md)
- **Time Complexity**: $O(1)$ per sample, but with a higher constant factor due to six interpolation calls and six arithmetic operations per sample.
- **Limitations**: Higher computational cost per sample; sensitive to interpolation quality; not suitable for very large volumes where memory is the primary bottleneck.
